pos.personaBrief: Pass and move was the base of the strategy (Wikipedia refs. 102-105), and Shankly said to be patient 'even if it takes 89 minutes' and to make 'the opposition do all the chasing' (1981). The ball was something to keep, not to give away to set up counters.

pro.personaBrief: He wanted players who 'control it instantly and give a forward pass' and to 'keep it simple', but also 'never pass to a red shirt in one direction when there are two in the other'. His post-Red Star remark that 'building from the back is the only way to play' suggests his side didn't play out short under pressure.

est.personaBrief: The team 'played in sections of the field, like a relay', with the work shared out and nobody running the length of the pitch. Five-a-sides and the sweat box built short, close pass-and-move combinations ('short, neat passing movements' by 1973).

lar.personaBrief: Width came largely from overlapping full-backs (1974 final; Lawler's 61 goals from forays), and his ideal player was 'good in the air, and big with it'. Nothing shows a winger-dribble-and-cross philosophy.

blo.personaBrief: Effort to regain the ball was demanded ('work twice as hard as the opposition to get it back'), but the side also 'get behind it when they haven't' the ball, played containment away, and saved energy by making opponents chase.

mar.personaBrief: No source says zone or man. Yeats's 'never the ball and the man' and his duel-winning point to individual responsibility, while the relay-section structure and Lawler 'reading the game' point to defenders holding their areas, and Shankly was 'only concerned about us'.

pla.personaBrief: Shankly: 'we were only concerned about us and our collective approach', with patience until the goal comes. The only adaptation on record is containment away in European ties.

res.personaBrief: Winning came first for him ('much more important than' life and death). Liverpool were 'happy to contain teams and sit on slender leads' and contained away from home, even with a pass-and-move style.

sis.personaBrief: The collective comes first: 'eleven captains', 'everyone working for each other', 'the work was shared out'. There was 'room for individuals within our system', but no exemptions from the work.

jog.personaBrief: His ideal was 'two good feet, good in the air, and big with it' (Yeats), in the 'fittest side in the league', but he also wanted players who 'control it instantly'. So he asked for both technique and physicality, and everybody had to work.

bas.personaBrief: He built through signings (Yeats, St John, later Keegan, Toshack, Clemence) and was loyal to veterans, keeping the old side together 'too long' until Watford in 1970. After that he rebuilt with younger players and learned that 'you constantly change the team'.

lid.personaBrief: He was the clear boss who 'rammed it into us', and he released apprentices who didn't work hard. Paisley also called him 'a softie at heart' who wouldn't drop loyal players, and he built a 'we have twenty' group spirit.
